cim: Fayetteville School Board members review potential updated AI policy at October board meeting - Northwest Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
cim_eredeti: Fayetteville School Board members review potential updated AI policy at October board meeting - Northwest Arkansas Democrat-Gazette
szoveg_eredeti:
FAYETTEVILLE -- The School Board will be asked to review the district's new artificial intelligence policy at its November meeting.

Board members had their first opportunity to review the policy on Thursday and hear about how it could change before final approval.

The policy, as it stands, is intended to ensure safe and responsible use of the technology, foster innovation in instruction, and promote operational efficiency, while establishing clear expectations for AI use, according to a draft presented Thursday night.

Act 848, passed into law in 2025, requires all public entities in Arkansas to establish policies and training requirements for employees using artificial intelligence and automated decision tools.

Claire Wilkinson, the district's general counsel, said leaders throughout the district spent the last year drafting an artificial intelligence policy that the School Board previously adopted. She said officials with the state's Department of Elementary and Secondary Education then crafted their own lengthy, detailed policy with directives that districts were required to adopt as well.

"So what we have attempted to do is merge the required DESE policy with the policy that we, you know, custom made and tailored for our district," Wilkinson told the board.

She said she still has questions about the state's policy, specifically in regard to requirements for contracts with companies providing artificial intelligence software. The Arkansas School Boards Association is also in the process of creating its own model policy, which Wilkinson said the district could look to for guidance for changing its own policy.

One key aspect of the policy outlines privacy protection for students and employees. Anyone using AI must use a program selected in alignment with the state K-12 cybersecurity policy and the Student Data Vendor Security Act. Educators must comply with the state's educator code of ethics as well as the district's code of ethics, according to the draft policy presented Thursday.

Confidential student or personnel data cannot be input into public or unapproved AI tools, and these tools cannot be the sole basis for decisions that significantly affect students, such as assigning grades.

The policy also notes that the district must ensure that AI is used to support student learning and not used as a replacement for instruction of students. It outlines that any software used must not limit the completion of assignments by students. Any chosen program must also allow teachers to disable AI features for specific assignments, have moderation mechanisms for detecting unsafe interactions and block access to inappropriate content.

The policy also notes the district must ensure that AI tools used by the district limit unnecessarily human-like behaviors, do not engage in personal or emotional relationships with students and do not use manipulative practices intended to promote excessive use of these tools.

Researchers at Common Sense Media found in June while 86% of children use AI, and nearly a quarter do so every day, more than 4 in 10 kids say no trusted figure has ever talked with them about AI safety.

Apps like ChatGPT and Character.ai have been criticized by researchers for engaging in manipulative actions. Researchers at Penn State found that AI-powered chatbots can become too agreeable with their users over time. This behavior, better known as sycophancy, can reduce the chatbot's accuracy over time by causing it to agree with users even when they are wrong about a topic.

Some AI apps not tailored for educational purposes can create emotional reliance or push behaviors such as emotional dependence, exacerbation of mental illness, and self-harm, according to researchers at Northeastern University.

Wrongful death lawsuits against ChatGPT's developer, OpenAI, have alleged a lack of guardrails with the company's product. In one case, a 31-year-old Washington woman allegedly died after the chatbot coached her on how to taper off her seizure medication against her doctor's advice. In another, a California family alleged their son died by suicide and that the app actively discouraged him from disclosing his mental health issues to loved ones.

A spokesperson for OpenAI even acknowledged in a statement last year that prolonged use of the app can allow users to skirt around certain safeguards meant to keep younger users safe.

Public entities like the School District are then left to create AI regulation policies themselves, working to protect students while also trying to explore how the tools can aid students, educators and administrators. Wilkinson acknowledged the district was in uncharted territory, noting that board members will likely have questions about the policy before it is put into place.

The draft of an updated policy was introduced Thursday night as new business, meaning the School Board will not consider voting on its approval or denial until their November meeting.

Miceala Morano can be reached by email at mmorano@nwaonline.com.

Miceala Morano covers education news for the Northwest Arkansas Democrat-Gazette. She is a lifelong Arkansan who earned a degree in multimedia journalism from the University of Arkansas in Fayetteville. She began her journalism career writing for the university’s newspaper, the Arkansas Traveler, where she covered breaking news, nonprofits and politics. She interned and wrote freelance pieces for the Democrat-Gazette during college and returned after graduation to cover news on her home turf.
